title: Japan’s Hayabusa2 Abort Asteroid Landing After Engine Failure, Shifts Mission Plans
body:
Japan’s space agency JAXA has scrapped its original plan to rendezvous with the tiny near‑Earth asteroid 1998 KY26, opting instead for a rapid fly‑by of a different space rock, 2015 BM510. The change comes after engineers identified a critical malfunction in the ion‑thruster system of the Hayabusa2 spacecraft, a problem that would have made the precise orbital insertion required for a landing impossible without risking the probe’s safety. By redirecting the probe to a high‑speed encounter, JAXA hopes to still harvest valuable scientific data while preserving the spacecraft for future missions.

Hayabusa2, launched in 2014, earned international acclaim for its successful sample‑return mission to the carbon‑rich asteroid Ryugu in 2019, marking the first time material from a primitive asteroid was brought back to Earth. After completing its primary objectives, the probe entered an extended‑mission phase, during which JAXA plotted a daring rendezvous with 1998 KY26—a mere 30‑meter‑wide rock that orbits the Sun faster than any known asteroid. The mission would have tested the limits of autonomous navigation and deep‑space propulsion, potentially paving the way for future asteroid‑deflection or resource‑extraction endeavors.

However, during routine diagnostics in early September, mission controllers detected a drop in thrust output from the spacecraft’s xenon ion engine, a key component for the delicate maneuvers required to match velocities with 1998 KY26. The engine’s performance fell short of the margins needed for a safe orbital insertion, and the risk of a missed approach or uncontrolled drift became unacceptable. “Our priority is the integrity of the spacecraft and the safety of the mission,” said Hiroshi Yamaguchi, JAXA’s deputy project manager. “Given the engine’s condition, a full rendezvous would have entailed a high probability of failure, which we cannot justify after the remarkable achievements already accomplished.”

In light of the technical constraints, JAXA re‑targeted Hayabusa2 to perform a close fly‑by of 2015 BM510, an asteroid roughly 400 meters across that will pass within 5,000 kilometers of Earth later this year. While the encounter will be brief—lasting only a few minutes at a relative speed of about 12 km/s—it still offers a unique scientific opportunity. The spacecraft’s suite of instruments, including a near‑infrared spectrometer, a lidar altimeter, and a high‑resolution camera, can capture surface composition, topography, and thermal properties of the asteroid. These data will augment existing catalogs of near‑Earth objects (NEOs) and improve models of how such bodies evolve under solar radiation and gravitational influences.

The pivot also underscores the broader challenges of long‑duration deep‑space missions. Ion thrusters, prized for their fuel efficiency, are susceptible to gradual wear and contamination, especially after years of exposure to the harsh space environment. Engineers are now reviewing the performance logs to better predict degradation patterns for future spacecraft, such as the upcoming MMX (Martian Moons eXploration) mission that will also rely on electric propulsion. Moreover, the decision reflects a growing emphasis on mission resilience: rather than abandoning a spacecraft entirely when a primary objective becomes unattainable, agencies are increasingly designing flexible trajectories that can be adapted on the fly.

Looking ahead, JAXA plans to keep Hayabusa2 operational for as long as its subsystems remain healthy, potentially targeting additional fly‑bys of other NEOs in the coming years. The data gathered from 2015 BM510 will feed into international efforts to refine asteroid impact risk assessments and may inform future endeavors to mine or redirect small asteroids. Although the dream of landing on the ultra‑fast 1998 KY26 will have to wait for a more robust platform, the agency’s swift re‑planning demonstrates both the ingenuity and the caution that define modern space exploration.
